belittle|disparage.distinction: Belittle makes something sound small, while disparage runs it down in words to lower everyone else's opinion of it.

belligerent|pugnacious.distinction: A belligerent person or country is already hostile, while a pugnacious one is simply eager to pick a fight.

belligerent|truculent.distinction: Belligerent is aggression already in motion, while truculent is a defiant readiness to fight that shows in the manner.

bemoan|lament.distinction: Bemoan is complaining regret about how things are, while lament is fuller mourning, usually for something or someone lost.

berate|chide.distinction: Berate is angry scolding at length, while chide is a mild reproof that stops well short of anger.

beseech|conjure.distinction: Beseech is begging urgently, while conjure calls something up as if by magic, and only rarely means to entreat solemnly.

beseech|entreat.distinction: Beseech is the more urgent and anguished asking, while entreat is earnest and humble, quieter in tone.

beseech|supplicate.distinction: Beseech is urgent begging of anyone at all, while supplicate carries the posture of kneeling before someone with power.

besiege|circumvent.distinction: Besiege surrounds an obstacle and presses hard on it, while circumvent goes round it and avoids the fight entirely.

besmirch|denigrate.distinction: Besmirch stains a reputation, often by mere association, while denigrate attacks it directly in words.

besmirch|slander.distinction: Besmirch is any staining of a good name, while slander is the specific spoken falsehood, and a legal wrong.

besmirch|sully.distinction: Besmirch and sully both stain a name; besmirch is the public smearing, sully the quieter loss of purity.

bestow|impart.distinction: Bestow hands over a gift or an honour, while impart passes on something less tangible, like knowledge or a flavour.

betoken|foreshadow.distinction: Betoken is a present sign of what is already the case, while foreshadow points forward to an event still to come.

bilious|dyspeptic.distinction: Bilious is bad temper with a sour liverish edge, while dyspeptic is irritable gloom, named from indigestion.

bilk|fleece.distinction: Bilk cheats someone out of what they are owed, while fleece strips a customer bare by overcharging them.

bilk|foil.distinction: Bilk cheats a person out of money, while foil simply stops a plan from succeeding.

bilk|frustrate.distinction: Bilk takes money by cheating, while frustrate blocks an effort without any money changing hands.

bilk|swindle.distinction: Bilk and swindle both cheat someone of money; swindle is the broad confidence trick, bilk often a failure to pay what is due.

bland|insipid.distinction: Bland is simply without flavour or edge, while insipid says the same thing with contempt, of food or of art.
